articles.title: I Built a Tool That Shows You How Much Money You're Losing Per Minute of Downtime
articles.excerpt: The problem that started it: I was running a small side project and my site went down for 2 hours before I noticed. I checked my uptime tool — it had pinged me. I'd missed the notification. When I loo…
articles.body: The problem that started it: I was running a small side project and my site went down for 2 hours before I noticed. I checked my uptime tool — it had pinged me. I'd missed the notification. When I looked at my revenue logs afterward, I could see the exact hole. I thought: why isn't this data in the monitor itself? What existing tools get wrong: Standard uptime monitors treat downtime as an ops problem. They tell you a binary state: up or down. But for any site generating revenue, the real question is "what's this costing me?" — and no one was answering that. What I built: SiteBleed™ — uptime + SSL monitoring with live revenue-loss tracking.

articles.title: Why Your CI Agent Can't Install pip
articles.excerpt: If you've ever set up a self-hosted CI/CD agent on a fresh Ubuntu image and hit pip: command not found or No module named pip, your first instinct is probably to check the network. Mine was too. That…
articles.body: If you've ever set up a self-hosted CI/CD agent on a fresh Ubuntu image and hit pip: command not found or No module named pip , your first instinct is probably to check the network. Mine was too. That instinct is wrong, and the real answer took me four attempts to actually land on. Here's the full story, including the three dead ends, because I think the dead ends are the useful part. The setup A self-hosted CI agent (in my case, an Azure DevOps agent, but this applies just as much to a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner or a plain Jenkins box) running on a minimal Ubuntu image. No sudo access on the box that's deliberate, since the agent shouldn't need root just to run a pipeline. I needed to install a CLI tool that only ships via pip .

articles.title: Embedding JPG Snapshots in a Production PDF Pipeline Without Breaking a11y or Print Layout
articles.excerpt: You already have an automated report pipeline that emits PDF invoices, contracts, or inspections. One day product asks: "Can we also drop in the photographer's JPG from the site visit, or the customer…
articles.body: You already have an automated report pipeline that emits PDF invoices, contracts, or inspections. One day product asks: "Can we also drop in the photographer's JPG from the site visit, or the customer's signature image?" The conversion is trivial. The blast radius is not. A naive "merge the JPG into the PDF" solution leaks through to receipts, screen readers, and print drivers in ways that only show up weeks later. This article is for the engineer who has to plug that requirement in today, not the document specialist who gets a week to plan it. The Real Problem Is Not "JPG to PDF" Calling this a "JPG to PDF conversion" is the first framing mistake. Almost no real product asks the user to upload JPGs and download a PDF.

articles.title: From One Task to a Working Agent: Trigger, Data, Action, Deliver
articles.excerpt: "Agent" is doing too much work The word "agent" now covers almost anything. A single chat prompt gets called an agent. A cron job with an LLM in the middle gets called an agent. So does a system that…
articles.body: "Agent" is doing too much work The word "agent" now covers almost anything. A single chat prompt gets called an agent. A cron job with an LLM in the middle gets called an agent. So does a system that plans, calls ten tools, and retries on failure. Strip the branding and most useful agents share the same small shape: something happens, the system gathers what it needs, does the work, and puts the result where a human or another system will see it. Four steps: trigger, data, action, deliver. If you can name each step for your use case, you can build it. If you can't, you don't have an agent yet, you have a vague hope.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starship megarocket makes the 'softest splashdown' ever after launching next-gen Starlink satellites in Flight 13 test (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched Starship, the world's most powerful rocket, on a critical 13th test flight on July 24, a stunning test flight that notched big success and ended with a huge surprise.
articles.body: SpaceX launched the world's most powerful rocket on a critical 13th test flight late Friday, but there was no triskaidekaphobia on this mission. The July 24 test launch, Space's Starship Flight 13 mission , sent a towering rocket the size of a 40-story skyscraper into space from South Texas, returned its massive Booster to Earth, and then — in a feat perhaps none saw coming — gently landed its Starship upper stage in the Indian Ocean, where it tipped over to float belly up on the sea. "Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!" SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X . SpaceX's Starship Flight 13 test flight lifts off from Starbase, Texas on July 24, 2026.
